newsitem.title: USA: Central bankers look to low inflation for growth.
newsitem.headline: Central bankers look to low inflation for growth.

text.p: Central bankers, having abandoned the idea that inflation can lower unemployment, are focusing on the opposite notion -- that low inflation actually results in higher growth, Federal Reserve sources said.

"All of these central bankers have accepted to voluntarily keep a financial environment such that inflation is low enough not to figure as the basis on which business decisions and growth depend," a Fed source told Reuters on Tuesday.
The source noted that this view was widely espoused at a Kansas City Fed conference on inflation this weekend.

"Not only central bankers but Treasury officials have come to recognize how important it is to keep inflation low," the source said. "This means the old Keynesian version on how to exploit a tradeoff (between inflation and growth) has been debunked by modern economists."
The source said the potential outcome of the upcoming Fed policy meeting was not discussed at the conference.

"What was discussed is that it's very important for a central bank to forecast inflation, not just in the near term, but out in the future, and use that as the fulcrum from which monetary policy can be conducted," the source added.

The source said the inflation debate has now moved to a different approach where a group of economists, notably at the New York Fed, supported the view that low inflation fosters higher growth, and thus employment.

"I don't think there is any question about the Phillips Curve (about the inflation/unemployment tradeoff). Except at exceedingly low levels of inflation, no one (central banker) accepts the notion there is a Phillips Curve tradeoff."
The source stressed that, "actually, there are a number of people who find there is a relatively small but significant impact of stable prices on real growth."

The source said one research paper attracting central bankers' attention says that bringing the U.S. "inflation rate from 3.0 percent to 1.0 percent would add to the level of national output in the amount of about one percent of the Gross National Product."
"That (low inflation) does not change the growth rate, but it changes the aggregate level," the source said.

"Very few people would think we can sustain a growth rate of 4.8 percent in real terms and 6.7 percent in nominal terms without this resulting from a subtantial increase in inflation, which is what we don't want," the source stressed.

Another Fed source pointed to a March speech by New York Fed President William McDonough that says price stability should be regarded as being attained when the Consumer Price Index is in a 0.5- to 2.0-percent range."
"This accounts for the potential bias in the CPI," the source added, while stressing that such a level is regarded as achievable without putting too much strain on the economy.

McDonough also made the point last spring the Fed does not peg monetary policy to the unemployment rate, "otherwise we would not have lowered rates as we did," easing three times with a jobless rate at around 5.6 percent.

A third Fed source said the absence of a marked slowdown in the third quarter raised the question about whether demand is currently generating inflation, or whether the gap between inflation and nominal GDP is closing, due to higher productivity.
